paragraphs.source_en: My story: It has never been about retirement

units.source_en: My story: It has never been about retirement

paragraphs.source_en: For me, the pursuit of financial independence has never been about retirement. I like working and I’ve enjoyed my career. It’s been about having options. It’s been about being able to say “no.” It’s been about having F-You Money and the freedom it provides.

It’s been about being able to say “no.” It’s been about having F-You Money and the freedom it provides.

paragraphs.source_en: I started working when I was 13; even earlier if you count selling flyswatters door-to-door and collecting pop bottles from the side of the road for the deposits. For the most part, I’ve enjoyed work and I’ve always loved being paid.

units.source_en: I started working when I was 13; even earlier if you count selling flyswatters door-to-door and collecting pop bottles from the side of the road for the deposits.
For the most part, I’ve enjoyed work and I’ve always loved being paid.

paragraphs.source_en: From the beginning, I was a natural saver. Watching my money grow was intoxicating. I’ve never been sure how this started. It might be hardwired into my genes. It might be my mother seducing me with the image of the red convertible I’d be able to buy when I turned 16. But that was not to be.

paragraphs.source_en: My father’s health failed before that birthday and shortly thereafter so did his business. My savings went to pay for college and I learned it is a fiscally insecure world. Convertibles came later. To this day it stuns me to read about some middle-aged guy laid off from his job of twenty years and almost instantly broke. How does anyone let that happen? It is the result of failing to master money.

paragraphs.source_en: Long before I heard the term, I knew I wanted F-You Money. If memory serves, the phrase originates in James Clavell’s novel *Noble House*, and from the moment I read it, my goal had a tangible form and an unforgettable name.

paragraphs.source_en: In the novel, a young woman is on a quest to secure her own “F-You Money.” By this, she means enough money to be completely free of the demands of others and able to do exactly what she wants with her life and time. She’s after 10 million, far more than it takes to reach simple financial independence. At least for me. It helps to have a bit of the monk inside.

paragraphs.source_en: The other thing I quickly figured out is that financial independence is at least as much about being able to live modestly as it is about cash, as our opening parable describes.

paragraphs.source_en: Unlike in the novel, for me enough F-You Money isn’t necessarily enough to live on for the rest of your life. Sometimes it’s only just enough to step to the side for a while. I first had mine at age 25 when I’d managed to save the princely sum of $5,000; something achieved after working two years at $10,000 per year.
